comments.name: Ima Palled
comments.body:
When I was a kid, my grandfather used to send me audio letters on cassette tapes. He never broke the habit of speaking into the tape recorder as he would when talking into his Dictaphone for a secretary to later transcribe into a typed, paper letter. His audio letters thus sounded like this: 

"Hope you are having fun at camp (period). Yesterday (comma), your grandmother and I visited Sheila (comma), whose first question was (open quotation marks), "How are the grandchildren (question mark, close quotation marks)?" 

"(Paragraph) Looking forward to seeing you soon (exclamation point, period.)" 

Anyone who ever heard and remembers the kind of dictation that was necessary sixty years ago can appreciate the role that artificial intelligence has in allowing Whispr Flow and similar applications to more easily and intuitively convert text to speech. Note, though, that my grandfather was dictating simple business letters to his secretary via a machine that allowed him to work when she was not present; he was knowingly not composing great literature. There is a valid place for technologal aid such as this, so long as one understands the proper use and limits of the technology. Those who are sufficiently naive as to believe that stream-of-consciousness dictation equals great writing do so at our collective cultural peril.

For the benefit of the readers, these talks aren't solely about trade; they are about whether Canada will be a self-governing country with agency over its economy, or a vassal state to the US. There is much of the latter already and that explains the objectionably imperious attitude of the US negotiators. 

The American Ambassador to Canada, unpopular as he may be, has had the virtue of periodic clarity about what the REAL issues are: (1) priority access to Canadian rare minerals, (2) exclusivity at a discount on Canadian oil, (3) the F-35 fighter jet contract, (4) the restoration of American booze on the shelves of the liquor commissions, and (5) the dismantling of dairy supply management in Canada as needed for unfettered US access to the Canadian dairy market. There may be others, but those are the key ones, and they strike at the heart of Canada's economic sovereignty. 

As well Canada is loathe to make piece-meal concessions that pit one province against the other, given how regionally-based various Canadian industries happen to be. That is why Canada needs a comprehensive agreement - to keep the country together, contrary to the US interest to dismember it. 

Also important is a serious question about whether anything signed with this Administration will be respected, and how an agreement can provide perfected security about that. 

This is the real meat of what's going on. It's much less about 50% tariffs on hockey sticks.

People wear head scarves for all sorts of reasons - style, comfort, religion, and yes to cover illness-related hair loss (which not only includes cancer but also diseases like alopecia). comments.name: Walter Stellenbosch
comments.body:
My thoughts are these, and they concern economic strength and the power that emerges from it: 40 years ago China was just beginning to emerge from the backwater it had been for well over a century; and, today it competes quite successfully with the advanced economies of the West. 

Additionally, China's economic strength continues to steadily grow; this despite nascent but growing efforts in the West to slow and, sometimes, to stymie that growth.

This takes place during a time when the Chinese state has significant economic issues of its own creation: a system built on substantial debt at every level; major financial calamites with the collapse of the property sector as the leading example; weak growth in consumer spending as Chinese people spend less in anticipation of even tougher times ahead; after years of layoffs due to remarkable improvements in manufacturing efficiency, China now has over 300 million gig workers; the social safety net in China is virtually non-existent compared to what we in the West enjoy (hence the increasing unwillingness to spend beyond the basics); 200 million rural Chinese continue to live on an estimated $7.50 per day; and the list goes on.

The top-line issue remains that the CCP plans, intends, and fully expects to determine how the world is going to work in the coming decades. I wonder how many sane and informed Americans and Europeans would bet against that eventuality.

This is what we're facing, and Loudon County is one part of the story.

Also, the impact of Loudoun's data centers is bourn by residents in nearby counties, too, with transmission lines and substations that are serving data centers in. Loudoun. All ratepayers are paying for this infrastructure from which the data centers primarily benefit.

comments.body: I live in Loudoun County.  The statements by county officials praising data centers are misleading. A very small three bedroom house (which is vanishingly hard to find, since all the new housing is either McMansions or lavish townhouses) sells for $525,000.  Meanwhile these massive data centers are covering vast swaths of the eastern part of the county.  Western Loudoun is predominantly rural, and lacks the infrastructure for dense development ( plus zoning regulations preclude such development).  So citing a percentage of land covered by data centers is also highly misleading.  The data centers are being crammed into a very small land area.

When I arrived at university, luck would have it my first lecture on my first day was delivered by my politcal science professor. He passed out voter registration forms to everyone and said he'd fail anyone who did not show him evidence of voter registration or they we were not eligible. I never found out if he was serious or not as I was already registered. It turned out to be a great semester. More than forty years later, I still have not missed an election day.

comments.name: Linda
comments.body:
This is crazy. And bad. One of the main reasons the vote was extended to 18 year olds was the Vietnam War. People who were 18 years old could be drafted, sent to Vietnam to die, but could not vote.

I was alive then, though rather young. But unlike now, I watched the war every night on TV. I think we should return to that. We should keep our wars top of mind. We need to see what's really happening on the ground, and in the air, to understand the totality of the war.

When "Uncle Walter" Cronkite went on the air and said the Vietnam War was "mired in stalemate" and the only way out was through negotiation; it was Feb 27, 1968. America paid attention. The war became more unpopular and more Americans died.

Bobby Kennedy was still alive. LBJ had not quit his re-election bid yet and North Vietnam's Tet Offensive took some Americans by surprise. And some think it shouldn't have been a surprise. In addition we no longer have  a steady, fair and unbiased media like Walter Cronkite brought us. 

Now everything is viewed through a political lens, and it shouldn't be.
If you can't vote for, or against, a war you will have to fight in, how can that be fair? It isn't and the vote was extended to 18 year olds.

Not that much has changed since then when it comes to voting at 18. You are an adult in the eyes of the law: sign a contract or be arrested as an adult.
So the only reason to disenfranchise 18-20 year olds is purely political. And Trump feels that 18-20 year olds don't support him.

People have been using this medicine for centuries with great benefits and few drawbacks. The super high THC products (dabs, high THC gummies and vapes) are very new ways of getting high. Much like distilling whiskey or fermenting grapes for wine, there are various ways of extracting greater or lesser amounts of THC.  With time, experience, and some common sense regulation, my guess is that this issue can be worked out. Additionally, some part of the population will always overdue a substance. comments.body:
This article lacks a link to the actual JAMA study, relying on vague generalizations. It also ignores the Farm Bill’s role in flooding the market with unregulated, ultra-potent analogs like THC-P that bypass safety testing.

Furthermore, the report overlooks the medical reality of Cannabis Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS). While studies exist, public awareness is dangerously low, leaving many users unaware that cannabis can cause the very nausea they treat. By focusing solely on 'addiction' and ignoring these physiological risks, the media misses the mark.

Blaming 'cannabis' as a monolith without addressing the regulatory failure that allows these potent synthetics to flood the market, or the real physiological dangers like CHS, is misleading. Readers deserve transparency, a direct link to the source data, and a nuanced discussion that goes beyond alarmist headlines.

comments.body: Having owned both a condo and single family home, I can say it's much easier to forget about home maintenance when you own a condo because you are not responsible for it unless you're a board member.  And having been on my condo board I can say it was a real learning experience. Board members are not managers, accountants and building contractors all rolled into one.  They are volunteers and most of them have no professional experience in those areas.  I think the answer is to get advice from people who are  experts in the form of a reserve study.  That is a report from an expert in assessing the condition of both the structures and finances of the association.  They make recommendations about the expected life of the structural components, compare your expenses with other similar associations and make recommendations for a repair schedule and reserve fund amounts.  As insurance gets harder to come by and more expensive, having a reserve study and conforming to recommendations shows the insurance company that the building is well maintained and less likely to require expensive emergency repairs.  It also explains to owners why fees are increasing.  It costs money but it's money well spent.  As far as increasing damage due to climate change, that's a fact of life these days.

I do think your abortion stance conflicts with your concept of deciding for oneself as long as those decisions do not come at the expense of others' rights and freedoms.

It valued the rights of the pregnant woman (I am not ready or willing for whatever reason to have a baby or carry one--(my very wanted pregnancies were difficult, but I would never have had an abortion--and prior to the second trimester it is my righ tto terminate this pregnancy. It is not trivial to note that when Vance says “In hindsight, part of why Milton Friedman’s ideas made more sense in the 1980s is because they were being advocated in a country that still had a very rich and powerful institutional Christianity," he is ignoring the fact that Friedman, in fact, was raised Jewish, not Christian, and later identified as an agnostic.

This is more than a "gotcha." It illustrates the crucial point that, while it is not wrong to say, as John Adams did, that a free society cannot succeed without ethical constraints, it is fundamentally un-American to say that any one religion, or religion itself, has a monopoly on articulating those ethical constraints. Our Constitution leaves it to the individual to determine which ethical/religious system suits best, and enshrines into law those ethical and moral precepts that do not depend on religious dogma for their validity. A concept Friedman embraced wholeheartedly.

comments.name: Joe
comments.body: Just a couple of thoughts on this story.  Although fraudulent litigation is a national problem, it is endemic in the five boroughs of New York City where we have one-party rule.  Judges are elected, but getting the nomination of the party in charge usually means that the election is a mere formality.  No one gets the nomination (usually bestowed in a closed party convention) unless the plaintiffs' bar gives the okay.  The same requirement applies for appointments to the bench when there is a vacancy.  Judges are therefore beholden to plaintiffs' attorneys, as are most other elected official in this state.  Judges routinely ignore rules of procedure and statutory safeguards in order to favor plaintiffs; trial rulings consistently favor one side and punish the other; relevant evidence is kept from juries; fabricated opinion evidence is allowed, and appeals to higher courts linger for up to three years, thus enabling the worst kind of lawyers to prosper at the expense of justice.  It is little wonder then that New York City is deemed to be a "judicial hellhole", and that the costs of that honor is passed on to the rest of us.

comments.body: Will, I share your love of cemeteries. They are peaceful places, and often in the middle of beautiful gardens, parks, and are shady refuges in big cities. If you walk through a cemetery that has existed since the early 19th century, you will probably see some gravestones with young children buried there.  Many children that died as children in the 1800s and early 1900s died from diseases that are now preventable by childhood vaccinations.

Once we cleared the cemeteries we either in the woods or on the Elmira Reformatory property, which is another story.

I hadn't thought about how the lives of others had progressed until recently reading "The Story of Arthur Truluv" who goes to have lunch at his wife's grave daily and thinks about the lives of those surrounding her. I love cemeteries. Besides just wandering around cemeteries, I have taken two cemetery tours in Colorado Springs where actors in period costume tell the stories of those departed. My husband declined my invitation to go along.

As I toured the cemetery and heard stories of famous locals or of families wiped out from diseases that we now have vaccines for — TB, influenza, diphtheria, measles and so forth, I patted myself on the back for getting my vaccinations. Colorado Springs also had many tuberculosis sanitariums back in the day so those afflicted with TB, could convalesce in the dry air and sunshine that we are afforded here. Towards the end, I casually said to another solo woman on the tour, “Well if this isn’t a plug for getting your vaccinations, I don’t know what is.” But I suppose there is always that bus.

comments.name: Rebecca Martens

I beg any of those passing judgement to walk a mile in her shoes. As a former caregiver of a spouse who walked a very long, long road of illness... losing your partner while they are still there is a very difficult thing. Something almost impossible to truly explain. People in these situations make their own individual choices as to how to deal with it.
The depression that can take over when one becomes simply caregiver, breadwinner and parent can be overwhelming.  And before you say "get therapy, get meds" it isn't that simple. There is a hole in your life -- but that person is still there.
I know some who chose to find companionship and some who didn't. Dating is different in this situation, yes. I'm quite sure she is aware of that. Being able to simply be able to be open to a new relationship can be enough to begin to feel like a person again. 
For the LW - I recommend seeking out the Well Spouse organization on Facebook. You will find a great deal of support there.

In an ideal situation, the writer would seek agreement by her spouse, but, as that doesn’t seem possible, as long as she can meet her other obligations I’d encourage her to look for what she needs. Being with a ailing spouse or an ailing parent means having to  be the observer in order to help both. Honor thy father and mother or husband does not mean what most humans think. We have to grow spiritually and unfortunately "love" to humans means special love which to God is NOT love.

We have to learn to listen to the still small voice because we mistakenly think love requires sacrifice. Sacrifice is an idea of the inner critic who is not anyone's friend. 

We do not have to give in to the demands of another ego on our ego which is what both the wife and daughter are doing, but we do have to relate to spouses and parents/children as great Self to great Self, as it frees both instead of imprisons. 

Think of these situations as wake up calls which we humans need to come up higher to peace above earth' battleground. "Ask and you will receive" is the promise--the problem is the world teaches us to ask for what we don't want--as the inner foe uses fear and doubt to divide us against ourselves. The ensuing worry bring us exactly what we don't want--illness through a nunsound mind.

I do think it's too much of a job to have to take care of him 24/7, especially since his mind seems to be gone. It's extremely difficult to be around someone in that condition. Some areas go far too fast and produce anxiety, distractability, and sometimes angry acting out.  Other areas go too slowly and that results in depression.  A brain map, made by recording brain waves from the brain identifies areas that are either too sluggish or too speedy.  Treatment is by putting sensors over targeted areas and programming a computer to give a sensory "reward" when the bundle(s) of neurons in that area fire at the optimum speed, not too slowly, not too fast.  The reward can be a sound, a blink on a screen, or any perceptible stimulus.  It happens very fast and not by conscious control--the patient sits quietly, often watching tv, for 30-minute treatments with a trained professional.  Gradually the targeted neurons fire at the desired speed and the patient's experience does too--less lethargy, depression, or explosions, more positive mood.  It seems magical for children whose behavior is out of control--they watch a favorite tv show during treatments and gradually they stop acting out.  Adults "feel better" and can lead normal lives. All of this with NOTHING put into the body--no drugs, no shocks, no electricity introduced into the brain.  Just sensing what specific areas are doing and rewarding them for "doing better."   NFT saved my life after 70+ years of CPTSD craziness and suffering.   Google it!

Justice wasn't served (yet), but the youth is now paying more attention to what is happening in our homeland. I think that's a great step forward. May the force be with us.

comments.name: NoName
comments.body:
Thank you for your report on the incident regarding the Community Party official. This story highlights a significant concern for many of us living in Vietnam.
​Beyond the specific details of this crash, many citizens here feel a profound sense of helplessness when facing those in positions of power who often act with impunity. There is a widespread, systemic issue where individuals are frequently oppressed or silenced when they seek justice against those with authority.
​I am reaching out to express my hope that international media outlets like The New York Times will continue to investigate these patterns of behavior. By bringing broader visibility to the lack of accountability and the challenges faced by ordinary citizens in Vietnam, you can provide much-needed support for the cause of transparency and human rights. We hope such coverage encourages international oversight and prompts necessary reforms to ensure that no one is above the law.

comments.body: It is great to see Africans owning the value chain in lucrative industries, where they have mostly been suppliers of the raw materials that made the finished products they ended up buying from developed nations. I understand why some get repulsed by his riches, but to his credit, Dangote has been a catalyst and a partner in injecting capital into many viable initiatives in Africa. More than this article lists, Dangote is strategically helping alleviate African nations’ transportation and digital infrastructure needs, as well as dependence on food and energy imports.  His conglomerate is investing in multiple commercial data center hubs and power plants (Tanzania & Gambia), a sugar refinery in Nigeria, Africa’s largest fertilizer plant in Ethiopia, and fuel tank storage farms in Guinea and Djibouti. If the global crises send him the windfalls that make him richer, I commend him for his well-timed and strategic investments and wish him more success. Nigerians and the rest of Africans should rally around him and support any well-meaning homegrown investors by building the institutions and codifying laws that protect their investments for the long haul.

We now live in Italy and go to the beaches in Forte dei Marmi and I have to say, we prefer the beach clubs to all of the beaches we used to frequent.  A day at the beach in Forte dei Marmi is more than wonderful.  We park our car in the free  covered lot where it does not fry while you are on the beach. The only thing that needs to be carried is a small beach bag and even that is not really necessary since everything is provided for you at the beach clubs.......a tent with loungers, chairs, and a table, a lock box to store your personal items when you go swimming, huge fluffy beach towels, table service right on the beach and if you choose to eat lunch, a restaurant offering excellent local dishes, a personal changing cabana with with more fluffy towels with your own key, impeccably kept bathrooms alongside the cabanas, shaded seating areas to lounge in with oversized comfortable chairs and hammocks, and on top of all of that, a big, pristine pool to swim in. comments.body: Skepticism is healthy, and there indeed are some irresponsible tech company leaders showing glib indifference toward the principles of American democracy. So I understand concern. At the same time, half the voters in this country were well on the way to a stunning embrace of anti-democratic ideas and untruthful candidates largely through their personal choice to consume one-sided information from cable TV, chain emails, and online biased media sources that fail to follow any basic precepts of the Fourth Estate. Among my family and neighbors, those who cast votes in this manner haven’t been big users of AI. So while I understand the author’s concern around an AI authoritarian state, I think we have deeper problems that begin with each of us. I see the generally passive approach to media consumption as part of the problem—and perhaps also that so many of us are so overwhelmed by the challenges of just making a living and supporting families to track civic information effectively. If there’s any way to put AI in the service of citizens so they can pierce the propaganda bubbles and manage information overload, that would be a potential good thing. Going back to town meetings sounds fine—and we all should do that too. But in my experience over 40 years, those meetings can be quite problematic too. More often than we’d like to admit, such meetings offer an opportunity to witness up close how strident, disrespectful, and unkind we have become as a people.

As the spares self-destructed (Margaret, Andrew and Harry), there was glee on Fleet Street and a rush to stoke the downfall.  Even Charles as the Prince of Wales was tabloid fodder.  He was torn apart during the Diana soap opera years, while she was sanctified.  The amount of information Charles has announced about his cancer allows his diagnosis to lend itself to his public service message about the disease, while he also preserves his dignity and the dignity of his office.  The same goes for the Princess of Wales, who gets magnifying glass goings over of her body every time she appears in public.  She is lovely and people do stare at her outward presence, and that's quite enough voyeurism.  No need for nosy parkers to speculate about a missing womb or breast or whatever while passing off their intrusiveness as concern for her well being.

comments.name: Jim T.
comments.body: I am married to a Brazilian and lived in Sao Paulo for ten years. "Brazil is a country of the future, and always will be" is a well worn phrase wryly expressed by a population made cynical through never ending political false promises. As the article says, Brazil has vast potential and resources but corruption and crime rob the people of this bounty. These two very big problems cross party lines and impunity abounds. There's a huge corruption case going on now involving a banker and the many politicians he and his minions paid off, and it stretches from the Supreme Court on down. But it's just a repeat of past scandals and will be soon forgotten. Unless Brazil can muster the force to confront and stop corruption, from small town mayors on up, nothing will change and it won't matter who is in power. So sad for such a magical, wonderful culture and people.

comments.name: Sudhir Iyer
comments.body: This article does not mention the problems rising from the single largest minority stakeholder in Tata Trusts - the Shapoorji Pallonji (SP) group. They are heavily in debt despite having a share in Tata Sons several times larger than their debt. But they can't liquidate it easily to pay off their debt because Tata Sons is private. Either side (Tata Trust and SP group) does not want the other, but they cannot detach from each other that easily. SP group benefits heavily from public listing of Tata Sons. Tata Trusts will not want to go public however for reasons mentioned above - greater scrutiny and a hurry for short term profits that impatient public traders will be eyeing for.
